title: Meta battles political storm in India as Congress party sues, stages protests
html:
The case leaves Meta’s operations in India caught between the government and an opposition.

PHOTO: REUTERS

AI generated

NEW DELHI - India’s main opposition Congress party has sued Meta and the federal government, saying that an automated content-removal system is blocking political posts and images of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi ahead of state elections.

The filing takes a week-long Congress campaign against Meta from the streets to the courtroom, and highlights Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s automated takedown mandate, under which the Facebook and Instagram parent has restricted more than 5.4 million posts in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in all of 2025.

In a court filing dated Nov 25 in the Delhi High Court, seen by Reuters, Congress’ youth wing social media head Manu Jain said the rules have become “an instrument for the suppression of lawful political expression”.

The case leaves Meta’s operations in India, the company’s biggest market, caught between a government whose rules strip platforms of legal protection if they fail to comply, and an opposition demanding it push back.

Congress argues that Meta’s system is blocking posts that are not “exactly identical” copies of content previously ordered removed, including birthday greetings, tributes and a wedding invitation featuring Gandhi.

Meta says it moderates content in India in accordance with the law.

Meta declined to comment.

India’s IT and home ministries, which are named as co-respondents in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

Modi’s government has maintained that such laws are essential to prevent the proliferation of illegal and harmful content online in a market of over 1.1 billion internet users.

Congress is urging the court to strike down the mandate for automated takedowns and also order Meta to restore the posts, as well as disclose blocking criteria.

Hearings are expected to begin in the coming days.

‘Automated tools’ mandate

India amended its IT rules in February to require large platforms to use technical measures “including automated tools” to find and block any post “exactly identical” to content already removed under a court order or a written government notice.

Before that, platforms were asked only to “endeavour” to use such tools.

To comply, Meta has been restricting “100% identical copies of content, at scale and in country” under India’s amended IT rules, its transparency report shows.

The company says it is still testing and refining the system given the “unprecedented nature of this effort”.

Meta says it is required to automatically restrict content at scale in only a “limited” number of countries, which it says explains the higher volumes.

Congress says the automated system is catching far more than exact duplicates.

It is blocking birthday greetings, tributes and even a wedding invitation because they carry the photograph or name of opposition leader Gandhi, while “no order, notice, reason or even a ‘legal request’ has been disclosed,” the petition said.

In one case cited in the petition, a Nov 8 birthday greeting from a youth wing leader to a colleague, showing the colleague standing beside Gandhi, was blocked the same day.

“We restricted access to this content through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements,” the notice to the user read.

India is also one of seven markets, including Brazil and Hong Kong, where Meta does not tell users which government authority sought a restriction, citing “legal obligations and regulatory considerations”, its transparency report shows. Elsewhere, it does so in most cases.

Winder offensive by Congress

The automated takedown system “distorts the level playing field” needed for a free and fair election, especially as party workers rely on Meta’s platforms to reach voters ahead of state polls due early next year, the petition says.

Facebook and Instagram have 400 million and 515 million users respectively in India, according to research firm DataReportal.

Congress has put up large hoardings in several cities depicting Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg in the traditional uniform of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the ideological parent of Modi’s party.

An altered image of Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg during a campaign by Karnataka’s Youth Congress party in Bengaluru on Nov 24.

PHOTO: AFP

Congress’ youth wing has protested near Meta offices and clashed with police in several cities in recent days.

The BJP has accused the protesters of vandalising the offices of private companies.

At a closed-door meeting this week reported by Reuters, Congress told Meta to push back against first-instance takedown orders, as Elon Musk’s X has done, a source told Reuters.

X is currently engaged in a legal battle against the government over its content-removal system.

Meta told Congress at the meeting that it is neutral towards all political parties and bound by local laws. REUTERS
summary: Hearings are expected to begin in the coming days.
